The name and lexical reconstruction are debated. UT's Krause-based chart gives perþō and ‘fruit tree’; the corpus does not present this as settled.
The Elder form and its Old English Eolh-secg and Scandinavian Ýr descendants form a difficult, non-identical relationship; all three poem mappings are marked likely-related.

rune_poems.original_text:
Fé er frænda róg
ok flæðar viti
ok grafseiðs gata
rune_poems.locator: The Icelandic Rune Poem, stanza 1: Fé
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
Wealth is strife among kinsmen,
and the tide’s beacon,
and the serpent’s path.
rune_poems.translation_notes: The final two phrases are poetic circumlocutions for gold; their concrete images are retained instead of being flattened into a rune meaning.

rune_poems.original_text:
Úr er skýja grátr
ok skára þverrir
ok hirðis hatr.
rune_poems.locator: The Icelandic Rune Poem, stanza 2: Úr
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
Rain is the weeping of clouds,
and the ruin of the hay-harvest,
and the shepherd’s hatred.

rune_poems.original_text:
Þurs er kvenna kvöl
ok kletta búi
ok varðrúnar verr.
rune_poems.locator: The Icelandic Rune Poem, stanza 3: Þurs
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
A giant is women’s torment,
and a cliff-dweller,
and the husband of a giantess.

rune_poems.original_text:
Óss er algingautr
ok ásgarðs jöfurr,
ok valhallar vísi.
rune_poems.locator: The Icelandic Rune Poem, stanza 4: Óss
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
Óss is the aged Gautr,
and Ásgarðr’s prince,
and Valhöll’s ruler.
rune_poems.translation_notes: Gautr is retained as a name of Óðinn; translating Óss simply as “god” would erase the stanza’s specific naming.

rune_poems.original_text:
Reið er sitjandi sæla
ok snúðig ferð
ok jórs erfiði.
rune_poems.locator: The Icelandic Rune Poem, stanza 5: Reið
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
Riding is seated happiness,
and a swift journey,
and a horse’s labor.

rune_poems.original_text:
Kaun er barna böl
ok bardaga [för]
ok holdfúa hús.
rune_poems.locator: The Icelandic Rune Poem, stanza 6: Kaun
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
An ulcer is children’s affliction,
and a battle’s journey,
and a house of decaying flesh.
rune_poems.translation_notes: The bracketed word in the historical transcription is an editorial supply; the translation follows it without concealing that status.

rune_poems.original_text:
Hagall er kaldakorn
ok krapadrífa
ok snáka sótt.
rune_poems.locator: The Icelandic Rune Poem, stanza 7: Hagall
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
Hail is a cold grain,
and a shower of sleet,
and a sickness of snakes.

rune_poems.original_text:
Nauð er Þýjar þrá
ok þungr kostr
ok vássamlig verk.
rune_poems.locator: The Icelandic Rune Poem, stanza 8: Nauð
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
Need is a bondwoman’s longing,
and a difficult condition,
and wearisome work.

rune_poems.original_text:
Íss er árbörkr
ok unnar þak
ok feigra manna fár.
rune_poems.locator: The Icelandic Rune Poem, stanza 9: Íss
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
Ice is a river’s bark,
and the wave’s roof,
and peril to death-bound people.

rune_poems.original_text:
Ár er gumna góði
ok gott sumar
algróinn akr.
rune_poems.locator: The Icelandic Rune Poem, stanza 10: Ár
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
A fruitful year is people’s good,
and a good summer,
and a fully grown field.

rune_poems.original_text:
Sól er skýja skjöldr
ok skínandi röðull
ok ísa aldrtregi.
rune_poems.locator: The Icelandic Rune Poem, stanza 11: Sól
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
The sun is the clouds’ shield,
and a shining disk,
and the lifelong bane of ice.
rune_poems.translation_notes: Aldr-tregi is a compact personification of the sun as ice’s enduring grief or destruction; “lifelong bane” preserves that force.

rune_poems.original_text:
Týr er einhendr áss
ok ulfs leifar
ok hofa hilmir.
rune_poems.locator: The Icelandic Rune Poem, stanza 12: Týr
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
Týr is a one-handed god,
and the wolf’s leavings,
and ruler of temples.

rune_poems.original_text:
Bjarkan er laufgat lim
ok lítit tré
ok ungsamligr viðr.
rune_poems.locator: The Icelandic Rune Poem, stanza 13: Bjarkan
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
Birch is a leafy branch,
and a little tree,
and young-growing wood.
rune_poems.translation_notes: The Latin abies does not redefine the vernacular birch stanza; its separate gloss is preserved as part of the historical tag layer.

rune_poems.original_text:
Maðr er manns gaman
ok moldar auki
ok skipa skreytir.
rune_poems.locator: The Icelandic Rune Poem, stanza 14: Maðr
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
A person is a person’s joy,
and an increase of earth,
and an adornment of ships.

rune_poems.original_text:
Lögr er vellanda vatn
ok viðr ketill
ok glömmungr grund.
rune_poems.locator: The Icelandic Rune Poem, stanza 15: Lögr
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
Water is seething water,
and a broad kettle,
and the fishes’ land.
rune_poems.translation_notes: The stanza is built from poetic descriptions of water; glömmungr is understood contextually through the final land-kenning.

rune_poems.original_text:
Ýr er bendr bogi
ok brotgjarnt járn
ok fífu fárbauti.
rune_poems.locator: The Icelandic Rune Poem, stanza 16: Ýr
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Cautious descendant relationship; rune name, form, and poem lexeme are not identical across systems.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
Yew is a bent bow,
and brittle iron,
and the Fárbauti of the arrow.
rune_poems.translation_notes: Fífu fárbauti is an obscure kenning. Cleasby-Vigfusson gives fífa a literal plant sense and a poetic sense of arrow; the poetic sense fits this stanza, while Fárbauti remains unresolved.

rune_poems.original_text:
Fé vældr frænda róge;
føðesk ulfr í skóge.
rune_poems.locator: The Norwegian Rune Poem, stanza 1: Fé
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
Wealth causes strife among kinsmen;
the wolf grows up in the forest.

rune_poems.original_text:
Úr er af illu jarne;
opt løypr ræinn á hjarne.
rune_poems.locator: The Norwegian Rune Poem, stanza 2: Úr
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
Dross comes from poor iron;
the reindeer often runs over crusted snow.
rune_poems.translation_notes: Úr denotes slag or dross here, not the aurochs represented by the similarly named Old English rune.

rune_poems.original_text:
Þurs vældr kvinna kvillu;
kátr værðr fár af illu.
rune_poems.locator: The Norwegian Rune Poem, stanza 3: Þurs
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
A giant causes women anguish;
few become cheerful from misfortune.

rune_poems.original_text:
Óss er flæstra færða
fǫr; en skalpr er sværða.
rune_poems.locator: The Norwegian Rune Poem, stanza 4: Óss
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
An estuary is the way of most voyages;
a sheath is the way of swords.
rune_poems.translation_notes: The couplet is a compressed parallel: water journeys pass through an estuary as swords pass into a sheath.

rune_poems.original_text:
Ræið kveða rossom væsta;
Reginn sló sværðet bæzta.
rune_poems.locator: The Norwegian Rune Poem, stanza 5: Ræið
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
Riding, they say, is hardest for horses;
Reginn forged the finest sword.

rune_poems.original_text:
Kaun er barna bǫlvan;
bǫl gørver nán fǫlvan.
rune_poems.locator: The Norwegian Rune Poem, stanza 6: Kaun
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
An ulcer is an affliction to children;
suffering makes a corpse pale.
rune_poems.translation_notes: Kaun is a sore or ulcer. The second line’s bǫl is kept broadly as suffering rather than assigned a single cause of death.

rune_poems.original_text:
Hagall er kaldastr korna;
Kristr skóp hæimenn forna.
rune_poems.locator: The Norwegian Rune Poem, stanza 7: Hagall
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
Hail is the coldest of grains;
Christ created the ancient world.

rune_poems.original_text:
Nauðr gerer næppa koste;
nøktan kælr í froste.
rune_poems.locator: The Norwegian Rune Poem, stanza 8: Nauðr
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
Need makes for a narrow choice;
the naked freeze in frost.

rune_poems.original_text:
Ís kǫllum brú bræiða;
blindan þarf at læiða.
rune_poems.locator: The Norwegian Rune Poem, stanza 9: Ís
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
We call ice a broad bridge;
a blind person needs to be led.

rune_poems.original_text:
Ár er gumna góðe;
get ek at ǫrr var Fróðe.
rune_poems.locator: The Norwegian Rune Poem, stanza 10: Ár
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
A fruitful year is good for people;
I say that Fróði was generous.
rune_poems.translation_notes: Ár denotes a good or fruitful year rather than merely a unit of time.

rune_poems.original_text:
Sól er landa ljóme;
lúti ek helgum dóme.
rune_poems.locator: The Norwegian Rune Poem, stanza 11: Sól
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
The sun is the light of lands;
I bow to a holy judgment.

rune_poems.original_text:
Týr er æinendr ása;
opt værðr smiðr blása.
rune_poems.locator: The Norwegian Rune Poem, stanza 12: Týr
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
Týr is the one-handed god;
a smith often has to blow the bellows.

rune_poems.original_text:
Bjarkan er laufgrønstr líma;
Loki bar flærða tíma.
rune_poems.locator: The Norwegian Rune Poem, stanza 13: Bjarkan
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
Birch is the leaf-greenest of branches;
Loki gained prosperity through deceit.
rune_poems.translation_notes: Cleasby-Vigfusson records a figurative sense of tími as good fortune or prosperity. The terse construction and its mythic allusion remain uncertain.

rune_poems.original_text:
Maðr er moldar auki;
mikil er græip á hauki.
rune_poems.locator: The Norwegian Rune Poem, stanza 14: Maðr
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
A person is an increase of earth;
the hawk’s grip is great.

rune_poems.original_text:
Lǫgr er, fællr ór fjalle
foss; en gull ero nosser.
rune_poems.locator: The Norwegian Rune Poem, stanza 15: Lǫgr
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
A waterfall is water falling from a mountain;
gold is ornaments.
rune_poems.translation_notes: The gnomic parallel is intentionally kept terse; nosser denotes ornaments or treasures.

rune_poems.original_text:
Ýr er vetrgrønstr viða;
vænt er, er brennr, at sviða.
rune_poems.locator: The Norwegian Rune Poem, stanza 16: Ýr
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Cautious descendant relationship; rune name, form, and poem lexeme are not identical across systems.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
Yew is the greenest wood in winter;
when it burns, it is apt to scorch.
rune_poems.translation_notes: The second line may emphasize either the yew’s fierce burning or the likelihood of being scorched by it.

rune_poems.locator: The Anglo-Saxon Rune Poem, stanza 1: Feoh
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.

rune_poems.original_text:
Ur byþ anmod ond oferhyrned,
felafrecne deor, feohteþ mid hornum
mære morstapa; þæt is modig wuht.
rune_poems.locator: The Anglo-Saxon Rune Poem, stanza 2: Ur
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
The aurochs is resolute and high-horned,
a very fierce beast; it fights with its horns,
a renowned moor-strider—it is a courageous creature.
rune_poems.translation_notes: The animal is rendered as “aurochs”; the stanza emphasizes its ferocity and courage without treating those traits as divinatory meanings.

rune_poems.original_text:
Ðorn byþ ðearle scearp; ðegna gehwylcum
anfeng ys yfyl, ungemetum reþe
manna gehwelcum, ðe him mid resteð.
rune_poems.locator: The Anglo-Saxon Rune Poem, stanza 3: Ðorn
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
The thorn is exceedingly sharp; for every warrior
grasping it is harmful, immeasurably cruel
to every person who rests among it.

rune_poems.original_text:
Os byþ ordfruma ælere spræce,
wisdomes wraþu ond witena frofur
and eorla gehwam eadnys ond tohiht.
rune_poems.locator: The Anglo-Saxon Rune Poem, stanza 4: Os
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
The mouth is the source of every speech,
the support of wisdom and comfort of counselors,
and for every noble a blessing and hope.
rune_poems.translation_notes: Os is rendered contextually as “mouth” because the stanza concerns speech; this is not asserted as the reconstructed Elder Futhark rune name.

rune_poems.original_text:
Rad byþ on recyde rinca gehwylcum
sefte ond swiþhwæt, ðamðe sitteþ on ufan
meare mægenheardum ofer milpaþas.
rune_poems.locator: The Anglo-Saxon Rune Poem, stanza 5: Rad
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
Riding in the hall is easy for every warrior
and very bold for one who sits high
on a powerful horse over the mile-paths.
rune_poems.translation_notes: Bosworth-Toller gives swíþ-hwæt as very strong or very brave in this stanza. “Very bold” preserves that force; the contrast between indoor ease and an actual journey remains compressed.

rune_poems.original_text:
Cen byþ cwicera gehwam, cuþ on fyre
blac ond beorhtlic, byrneþ oftust
ðær hi æþelingas inne restaþ.
rune_poems.locator: The Anglo-Saxon Rune Poem, stanza 6: Cen
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
The torch is known to every living person by its fire,
pale and bright; it burns most often
where nobles rest indoors.
rune_poems.translation_notes: Blac can describe a pale, shining, or bright appearance; “pale” preserves the contrast with beorhtlic.

rune_poems.original_text:
Gyfu gumena byþ gleng and herenys,
wraþu and wyrþscype and wræcna gehwam
ar and ætwist, ðe byþ oþra leas.
rune_poems.locator: The Anglo-Saxon Rune Poem, stanza 7: Gyfu
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
Giving is an adornment and praise among people,
a support and a distinction; and to every exile
it is favor and sustenance when they lack all else.

rune_poems.original_text:
Wenne bruceþ, ðe can weana lyt
sares and sorge and him sylfa hæfþ
blæd and blysse and eac byrga geniht.
rune_poems.locator: The Anglo-Saxon Rune Poem, stanza 8: Wenne
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
Joy is enjoyed by one who knows little of want,
pain, and sorrow, and who possesses
prosperity and happiness and sufficient protection.
rune_poems.translation_notes: Byrga geniht literally suggests a sufficiency of strongholds or protections; the translation keeps the protective sense without forcing a concrete setting.

rune_poems.original_text:
Hægl byþ hwitust corna; hwyrft hit of heofones lyfte,
wealcaþ hit windes scura; weorþeþ hit to wætere syððan.
rune_poems.locator: The Anglo-Saxon Rune Poem, stanza 9: Hægl
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
Hail is the whitest of grains; it whirls from the sky’s air,
the wind’s showers toss it; afterward it turns to water.

rune_poems.original_text:
Nyd byþ nearu on breostan; weorþeþ hi þeah oft niþa bearnum
to helpe and to hæle gehwæþre, gif hi his hlystaþ æror.
rune_poems.locator: The Anglo-Saxon Rune Poem, stanza 10: Nyd
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
Need is a constriction in the breast; yet it often becomes for human children
both help and healing, if they heed it in time.

rune_poems.original_text:
Is byþ ofereald, ungemetum slidor,
glisnaþ glæshluttur gimmum gelicust,
flor forste geworuht, fæger ansyne.
rune_poems.locator: The Anglo-Saxon Rune Poem, stanza 11: Is
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.

rune_poems.original_text:
Ger byþ gumena hiht, ðonne God læteþ,
halig heofones cyning, hrusan syllan
beorhte bleda beornum ond ðearfum.
rune_poems.locator: The Anglo-Saxon Rune Poem, stanza 12: Ger
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
Harvest is people’s hope, when God—
holy king of heaven—allows the earth to give
bright fruits to nobles and to the needy.
rune_poems.translation_notes: Ger can denote the year and its yield; “harvest” fits the stanza’s emphasis on the earth’s produce.

rune_poems.original_text:
Eoh byþ utan unsmeþe treow,
heard hrusan fæst, hyrde fyres,
wyrtrumun underwreþyd, wyn on eþle.
rune_poems.locator: The Anglo-Saxon Rune Poem, stanza 13: Eoh
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
The yew is a rough-barked tree on the outside,
hard and fast in the earth, a guardian of fire,
supported by roots, a joy on the estate.
rune_poems.translation_notes: Hyrde fyres is retained relatively literally as “guardian of fire”; whether it points to the wood’s burning qualities or another association remains uncertain.

rune_poems.original_text:
Peorð byþ symble plega and hlehter
wlancum [on middum], ðar wigan sittaþ
on beorsele bliþe ætsomne.
rune_poems.locator: The Anglo-Saxon Rune Poem, stanza 14: Peorð
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
Peorð is always play and laughter
for the proud [in their midst], where warriors sit
together, cheerful in the beer-hall.
rune_poems.translation_notes: The referent of Peorð is uncertain, so the rune-name term is left untranslated. The brackets belong to the historical transcription.

rune_poems.original_text:
Eolh-secg eard hæfþ oftust on fenne
wexeð on wature, wundaþ grimme,
blode breneð beorna gehwylcne
ðe him ænigne onfeng gedeþ.
rune_poems.locator: The Anglo-Saxon Rune Poem, stanza 15: Eolh-secg
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Cautious descendant relationship; rune name, form, and poem lexeme are not identical across systems.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
The elk-sedge most often has its home in a fen;
it grows in water and wounds cruelly,
staining with blood every person
who makes any grasp at it.
rune_poems.translation_notes: The plant identity of eolh-secg and the exact force of blode breneð are disputed; the rendering preserves the cutting, blood-marking image.

rune_poems.original_text:
Sigel semannum symble biþ on hihte,
ðonne hi hine feriaþ ofer fisces beþ,
oþ hi brimhengest bringeþ to lande.
rune_poems.locator: The Anglo-Saxon Rune Poem, stanza 16: Sigel
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
The sun is always a hope to seafarers
when they carry it over the fishes’ bath,
until the sea-horse brings them to land.

rune_poems.original_text:
Tir biþ tacna sum, healdeð trywa wel
wiþ æþelingas; a biþ on færylde
ofer nihta genipu, næfre swiceþ.
rune_poems.locator: The Anglo-Saxon Rune Poem, stanza 17: Tir
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
Tir is a certain sign; it keeps faith well
with nobles; it is always on its course
over night’s mists and never fails.
rune_poems.translation_notes: The stanza describes a dependable celestial sign, but the translation does not identify it more narrowly where the text itself does not.

rune_poems.original_text:
Beorc byþ bleda leas, bereþ efne swa ðeah
tanas butan tudder, biþ on telgum wlitig,
heah on helme hrysted fægere,
geloden leafum, lyfte getenge.
rune_poems.locator: The Anglo-Saxon Rune Poem, stanza 18: Beorc
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
The birch is fruitless, yet it bears
shoots without seed; it is beautiful in its branches,
high in its crown, splendidly adorned,
laden with leaves, pressing toward the sky.

rune_poems.original_text:
Eh byþ for eorlum æþelinga wyn,
hors hofum wlanc, ðær him hæleþ ymb[e]
welege on wicgum wrixlaþ spræce
and biþ unstyllum æfre frofur.
rune_poems.locator: The Anglo-Saxon Rune Poem, stanza 19: Eh
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
The horse is, before nobles, the joy of princes,
a steed proud in its hooves, where around it wealthy heroes
on horses exchange words;
and it is always a comfort to the restless.

rune_poems.original_text:
Man byþ on myrgþe his magan leof:
sceal þeah anra gehwylc oðrum swican,
forðum drihten wyle dome sine
þæt earme flæsc eorþan betæcan.
rune_poems.locator: The Anglo-Saxon Rune Poem, stanza 20: Man
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
A person in happiness is dear to their kinsfolk;
yet each must betray the other,
because the Lord by his decree wills
to entrust the wretched flesh to the earth.

rune_poems.original_text:
Lagu byþ leodum langsum geþuht,
gif hi sculun neþan on nacan tealtum
and hi sæyþa swyþe bregaþ
and se brimhengest bridles ne gym[eð].
rune_poems.locator: The Anglo-Saxon Rune Poem, stanza 21: Lagu
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
The sea seems long-lasting to people
if they must venture in a tossing ship,
and the sea-waves greatly terrify them,
and the sea-horse does not heed its bridle.
rune_poems.translation_notes: Lagu broadly denotes water; “sea” is chosen here because the stanza’s ship, waves, and sea-horse establish a maritime setting.

rune_poems.original_text:
Ing wæs ærest mid East-Denum
gesewen secgun, oþ he siððan est
ofer wæg gewat; wæn æfter ran;
ðus Heardingas ðone hæle nemdun.
rune_poems.locator: The Anglo-Saxon Rune Poem, stanza 22: Ing
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
Ing was first seen among the East-Danes
by men, until afterward he went eastward
over the wave; his wagon ran after him.
Thus the Heardings named that hero.
rune_poems.translation_notes: The episode, the Heardings, and the direction expressed by est are textually and historically difficult; the translation preserves the narrative without supplying an identity or myth.

rune_poems.original_text:
Eþel byþ oferleof æghwylcum men,
gif he mot ðær rihtes and gerysena on
brucan on bolde bleadum oftast.
rune_poems.locator: The Anglo-Saxon Rune Poem, stanza 23: Eþel
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
An inherited estate is very dear to every person,
if there they may enjoy in their dwelling
what is right and fitting, most often with prosperity.

rune_poems.original_text:
Dæg byþ drihtnes sond, deore mannum,
mære metodes leoht, myrgþ and tohiht
eadgum and earmum, eallum brice.
rune_poems.locator: The Anglo-Saxon Rune Poem, stanza 24: Dæg
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Later-system rune correspondence; the poem remains evidence for its own named system, not an Elder Futhark definition.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
Day is the Lord’s messenger, dear to humankind,
the glorious light of the Creator, joy and hope
to the prosperous and the poor, useful to all.

rune_poems.original_text:
Ac byþ on eorþan elda bearnum
flæsces fodor, fereþ gelome
ofer ganotes bæþ; garsecg fandaþ
hwæþer ac hæbbe æþele treowe.
rune_poems.locator: The Anglo-Saxon Rune Poem, stanza 25: Ac
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Futhorc expansion rune with no canonical Elder Futhark position.
rune_poems.translation_notes: The opening compound image is compact and may refer to food or sustenance; the latter lines plainly evoke oak-built seafaring and the wood’s reliability.

rune_poems.original_text:
Æsc biþ oferheah, eldum dyre
stiþ on staþule, stede rihte hylt,
ðeah him feohtan on firas monige.
rune_poems.locator: The Anglo-Saxon Rune Poem, stanza 26: Æsc
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Futhorc expansion rune with no canonical Elder Futhark position.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
The ash is very tall, dear to people,
firm on its foundation; it holds its place rightly
though many people attack it.

rune_poems.original_text:
Yr byþ æþelinga and eorla gehwæs
wyn and wyrþmynd, byþ on wicge fæger,
fæstlic on færelde, fyrdgeatewa sum.
rune_poems.locator: The Anglo-Saxon Rune Poem, stanza 27: Yr
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Futhorc expansion rune with no canonical Elder Futhark position.
rune_poems.translation_notes: The object denoted by this Futhorc rune-name is uncertain in the stanza, so Yr is not replaced with a more specific implement.

rune_poems.original_text:
Iar byþ eafix and ðeah a bruceþ
fodres on foldan, hafaþ fægerne eard
wætre beworpen, ðær he wynnum leofaþ.
rune_poems.locator: The Anglo-Saxon Rune Poem, stanza 28: Iar
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Futhorc expansion rune with no canonical Elder Futhark position.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
Iar is a river-fish, and yet it always enjoys
food on land; it has a fair dwelling
surrounded by water, where it lives in delight.
rune_poems.translation_notes: The creature denoted by Iar is uncertain and apparently amphibious; the translation retains the source’s “river-fish” description rather than naming a species.

rune_poems.original_text:
Ear byþ egle eorla gehwylcun,
ðonn[e] fæstlice flæsc onginneþ,
hraw colian, hrusan ceosan
blac to gebeddan; bleda gedreosaþ,
wynna gewitaþ, wera geswicaþ.
rune_poems.locator: The Anglo-Saxon Rune Poem, stanza 29: Ear
rune_poems.mapping_justification: Futhorc expansion rune with no canonical Elder Futhark position.
rune_poems.editorial_translation:
The grave is dreadful to every noble,
when the flesh begins firmly—
the corpse—to cool and choose the earth,
pale, as a bedfellow; fruits fall,
joys depart, covenants cease.
rune_poems.translation_notes: Ear is rendered “grave” from the stanza’s context. The final wera can bear a covenant or pledge sense; the compressed ending remains open to nuance.
